title: Can Every Course Be Taken
statement:
A school offers n courses, numbered 0 to n - 1. Each entry rules[i] = [a, b] means course a must be finished before course b can start. You take one course at a time.

Return true if there is some order that lets you finish all n courses, and false otherwise. Rules may repeat, and a rule [a, a] means a course that needs itself.

examples.why: Course 2 needs both 1 and 3, and both of those need 0. Course 2 is reached along two routes, but that is not a loop: the order 0, 1, 3, 2 works.
Courses 1 and 2 each need the other first, so neither can ever start.
Course 1 needs itself, which is a loop of length one.

hints: Draw each rule as an arrow from a to b. When is it impossible to finish everything?
It is impossible exactly when the arrows contain a loop. So the question is: does this directed graph have a cycle?
Count, for each course, how many rules still block it. Start with every course that has 0, take it, and lower the count of everything it unlocks. If you manage to take all n courses there is no loop.

explain.intuition:
Draw every rule [a, b] as an arrow a → b. If the arrows form a loop, every course in the loop waits for another one in the loop, so none can start. If there is no loop, there is always some course with no arrows coming in, and taking it can only help. So the question is just: does this directed graph have a cycle? It is the same check a bundler makes before ordering modules by their imports.

Kahn's algorithm answers it by simulation. Keep, for each course, the number of rules still blocking it (its in-degree). Every course with in-degree 0 can be taken now; put those in a queue. Taking a course removes its outgoing arrows, which may drop other courses to 0. If the queue runs dry before all n courses are taken, the rest are stuck behind a loop. DFS with three colours is the other classic: a course is white (unseen), grey (on the current path) or black (finished). Meeting a grey course means you walked in a circle. A plain visited flag is not enough in a directed graph: in example 1, course 2 is reached twice without any loop.
steps: Build an adjacency list after[a] holding every b, and count indeg[b] for each rule.
Push every course with indeg = 0 into a queue.
Pop a course and count it as taken. For each b in its list, lower indeg[b]; when it reaches 0, push b.
Return whether the number of taken courses equals n.
pitfalls: Treating "reached twice" as a cycle. That is right for undirected graphs, but in a directed graph two routes into one course (example 1) are fine. DFS needs the grey state, not just a visited flag.

Ignoring duplicate rules or self-rules when counting in-degrees. A duplicate adds 2 to the in-degree and its two arrows remove 2, so counting every rule is correct. A self-rule [a, a] can never be removed, so a is stuck, as it should be.
Recursive DFS on a 50 000-course chain. It goes 50 000 calls deep and breaks Python's recursion limit, so the DFS below keeps its own stack.

solutions.title: Peel off ready courses, one sweep at a time
solutions.idea: Repeat: scan every rule to see which courses are still blocked, take every unblocked one, and stop when a sweep takes nothing. A long chain needs one sweep per course.

solutions.title: DFS with three colours (iterative)
solutions.idea: White = unseen, grey = on the current path, black = fully explored. An arrow into a grey course closes a loop. An explicit stack keeps deep chains safe.

solutions.title: Kahn's algorithm (BFS on in-degrees)
solutions.idea: Take courses whose in-degree is 0, removing their arrows as you go. If all n get taken, there is no loop.

followups: Return one valid order instead of true/false. What do you collect during Kahn's algorithm?
You can take up to k courses per term. What is the fewest number of terms? (Hint: BFS levels, if k is unlimited.)
